power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: South Africa's 2023 revised ART Guidelines moved the first scheduled viral load (VL) test from 6 to 3 months after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and accelerated differentiated care eligibility from 7 to 4 months among virally suppressed clients.
We assessed uptake of these changes and their association with virologic outcomes.

We analysed routine electronic medical record data from 18 primary healthcare clinics in three South African districts among all adults initiating or re-initiating ART (N=16,338; January 2022-March 2025).
Interrupted time series analyses were used to assess uptake of 3-month VL testing and assignment to ≥6month visit intervals following guideline implementation in April 2023.

Modified Poisson regression was used to compare relative risks (RRs) for viral suppression at the first and second routine VL tests among clients tested at 3 months (test window=56-111 days) and 6 months (112-<252 days).
text.formatted: Modified Poisson regression was used to compare relative risks (RRs) for viral suppression at the first and second routine VL tests among clients tested at 3 months (test window=56-111 days) and 6 months (112-<252 days).

text.text: At the first VL assessment, 27% of participants had VL tests at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; the rest had tests outside either window (19%) or no test documented (25%).
Three-month VL testing rose immediately after guideline implementation, reaching 72-85% coverage by the end of the study period.
Assignment to ≥6-month visit intervals among clients with 3-month viral suppression increased after implementation, reaching 48-71% across districts.
A second VL result was documented for 62% of clients tested in the 3-or 6-month window.
Viral suppression did not differ meaningfully between clients initially tested at 3 months (72%) and those initially tested at 6 months (72%).
Among clients with a second scheduled VL result, 82% were virally suppressed.
Assignment to ≥6-month visit intervals was not associated with subsequent viral suppression (aRR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.06).
Results should be interpreted with caution due to missing VL data.
South Africa's 2023 guideline revision was associated with rapid increases in 3-month VL testing and assignment to longer visit intervals.
Viral suppression at the first VL test was similar among clients tested at 3 and 6 months, and longer visit intervals were not associated with poorer outcomes.
These findings support earlier differentiation of HIV care within routine service delivery.
Incomplete uptake of recommended testing and visit intervals offers opportunities to strengthen implementation and warrants continued evaluation of longer-term outcomes.

Despite the tremendous progress of sub-Saharan Africa's HIV treatment programs in achieving very high levels of coverage with antiretroviral therapy (ART)(1), disengagement from care remains a major challenge to reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality, particularly during the first year after treatment initiation or re-initiation (2) (3) (4).
text.formatted: Despite the tremendous progress of sub-Saharan Africa's HIV treatment programs in achieving very high levels of coverage with antiretroviral therapy (ART)(1), disengagement from care remains a major challenge to reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality, particularly during the first year after treatment initiation or re-initiation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: In South Africa, home to the world's largest HIV treatment program, a recent analysis of routine medical record data from three provinces found that approximately one in six (16%) clients disengaged from care within six months of initiation, and only 59% remained continuously in care, with no treatment interruptions of greater than 28 days, during the first six months (5).
text.formatted: In South Africa, home to the world's largest HIV treatment program, a recent analysis of routine medical record data from three provinces found that approximately one in six (16%) clients disengaged from care within six months of initiation, and only 59% remained continuously in care, with no treatment interruptions of greater than 28 days, during the first six months <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: At 12 months, the corresponding figures were 23% and 45%.
Other countries, such as Zambia (6) and Malawi (7), face similar levels of disengagement and interruption.
text.formatted: Other countries, such as Zambia <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> and Malawi <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>, face similar levels of disengagement and interruption.

text.text: Over the past decade, many countries in the region have implemented policy and guideline changes designed to improve retention in care and reduce barriers to HIV treatment.
These include the introduction of differentiated service delivery (DSD) models (called differentiated models of care (DMOCs) in South Africa) and same-day ART initiation (SDI).

SDI has effectively eliminated loss to follow up between HIV testing and ART initiation for those who wish to start treatment (8), while DSD models such as community-based medication collection and multi-month dispensing intervals have reduced the burden of treatment on those who are "established" in care (9), typically defined as having at least 6 months' experience on ART and a suppressed viral load (VL).
text.formatted: SDI has effectively eliminated loss to follow up between HIV testing and ART initiation for those who wish to start treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>, while DSD models such as community-based medication collection and multi-month dispensing intervals have reduced the burden of treatment on those who are "established" in care <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>, typically defined as having at least 6 months' experience on ART and a suppressed viral load (VL).

text.text: While these policies successfully streamlined care for newly initiating and established clients (10, 11), only recently have changes been made that benefit those in the period between initiation and DMOC eligibility.
text.formatted: While these policies successfully streamlined care for newly initiating and established clients <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>, only recently have changes been made that benefit those in the period between initiation and DMOC eligibility.

text.text: The first six months after treatment initiation, known as the "early treatment period," have traditionally been characterized by frequent clinic visits and heightened risk of disengagement.
South Africa began to address this gap in 2023 with its revised Adherence Guidelines for HIV, TB and NCDs (12).
text.formatted: South Africa began to address this gap in 2023 with its revised Adherence Guidelines for HIV, TB and NCDs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: The new guidelines moved the first VL test to three months after initiation rather than six, made those with viral suppression at three months eligible for DMOC enrolment at four months rather than seven, and reduced the number of clinic visits required during the first year on treatment.
Taken together, these changes comprise a novel model of service for the early treatment period, a longstanding goal for service delivery innovation (13).
text.formatted: Taken together, these changes comprise a novel model of service for the early treatment period, a longstanding goal for service delivery innovation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: Although implementation began in 2023, little is known about the consequences of South Africa's guideline revisions for treatment outcomes.

In particular, it is unclear the extent to which facilities have adopted the three central changes most salient to the early treatment period-early VL testing, earlier enrolment in DMOCs, and fewer clinic visits-and whether these changes are associated with changes in viral suppression.
To assess this gap, we evaluated fidelity to and outcomes of these changes in the 2023 South African ART Guidelines.
We analysed routinely collected electronic medical record data to assess uptake of key guideline components and associated clinical outcomes.
The study was conducted at 18 public sector primary healthcare clinics (PHCs) in three South African provinces.
Six facilities were located in each of King Cetshwayo District (KC) in KwaZulu-Natal, Ehlanzeni District (EH) in Mpumalanga, and West Rand District (WR) in Gauteng.
All of these sites are part of the SENTINEL network, originally created in 2020 to monitor DMOC uptake and outcomes (14).
text.formatted: All of these sites are part of the SENTINEL network, originally created in 2020 to monitor DMOC uptake and outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Sites were selected to capture both urban and rural settings, the range of differentiated models of care being offered at that time, and assistance from diverse nongovernmental partner organizations supported by the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR).
The sites and the clients they serve have been described in several previous publications (14) (15) (16) (17) (18).
text.formatted: The sites and the clients they serve have been described in several previous publications <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Adult (≥18 years) clients who initiated or re-initiated ART at one of the study sites from January 1, 2022 onward were eligible for inclusion.
We excluded pregnant women, for whom treatment guidelines differ, but imposed no other restrictions at cohort entry.
Eligibility for the analytic cohort was subsequently restricted to clients with sufficient follow-up time to reach the final scheduled VL testing window.
Data were extracted from TIER.Net, South Africa's electronic medical record system for HIV treatment.
Variables extracted included demographic characteristics, ART regimens, ART initiation date, clinic visit dates, VL test dates and results, appointment dates, and prescription information.

Data were available from January 1, 2022 to April 30, 2026 for King Cetshwayo and Ehlanzeni districts and from January 1, 2022 to November 30, 2025 for West Rand District and were accessed on June 9 2026 for King Cetshwayo, May 9, 2026 for Ehlanzeni, and July 15, 2026 for West Rand.
For each patient, available follow-up time was determined individually based on their ART initiation date and the end of the available observation period.
The analytic cohort was restricted to patients with sufficient follow-up to reach the final scheduled VL testing window (at least 392 days).
TIER.Net includes a field for recording enrolment in DMOCs, but completion of this field was incomplete in the study dataset.

Recorded DMOC enrolment in the TIER.Net study dataset was substantially lower than estimates reported through routine programmatic monitoring and lower than levels observed in previous studies conducted at the same facilities.
We therefore used assignment to six-month clinic visits as a proxy measure of differentiated service delivery uptake.

Because clients may receive extended visit intervals without formal DMOC enrolment, this proxy measure may overestimate true DMOC enrolment, although it should provide a reasonable reflection of eligibility for differentiated service delivery at the four-month timepoint.

For this study, we focused on adherence to three core changes introduced in the 2023 guideline revision: 1) shifting of the first scheduled VL test from six months to three months after ART initiation; 2) shifting of eligibility assessment for six-month dispensing (3MMD), six-monthly clinic visits , and enrolment in a DMOC from seven months to four months after initiation (among clients who were virally suppressed); and 3) reduction in the recommended number of clinic visits in the first year from 11 to 6.
These changes are illustrated in Figure 1.

text.text: We note that the second scheduled VL test is recommended at 10 months after initiation for those whose first test is at 3 months and at 12 months for those whose first test is at 6 months (19).

text.text: Fidelity indicators and clinical outcomes

As measures of guideline fidelity, we assessed adherence to each of the three core components mentioned above: (1) uptake of VL testing approximately three months after ART initiation, defined as VL test observed in the EMR between two and four months after ART initiation; (2) assignment of virally suppressed clients to six-month clinic visit intervals as a proxy for DMOC enrolment; and (3) reduction in the number of clinic visits during the first year on ART, using a count of the number of clinic visits recorded during the first year after ART initiation.

Where multiple VL results occurred within a testing window, the result closest to the window's defined milestone (84, 182, 280, and 350 days for the 3-, 6-, 10-, and 12-month windows respectively) was selected.

For all VL endpoints (3 or 6 months and 10 or 12 months), VL was categorised as suppressed (<50 copies/mL), low-level viraemia (50-199 copies/mL), intermediate viraemia (200-999 copies/mL), or unsuppressed (≥1000 copies/mL).

text.text: To determine whether earlier VL testing at 3 months rather than 6 months was associated with treatment outcomes, we compared the proportion of clients achieving viral suppression at the first and second scheduled VL tests between those initially tested at 3 months and those initially tested at 6 months.

We defined the first scheduled VL test as a VL result documented within either the 3-month testing window (56-111 days after ART initiation) or the 6-month testing window (112-251 days after ART initiation) and the second scheduled VL result within the 10-month testing window (252-307 days) or 12-month testing window (308-391 days) after ART initiation.

To assess implementation of the revised six-monthly visit schedule, analyses were restricted to clients who achieved viral suppression (<50 copies/mL) at their first scheduled VL test, as viral suppression was an eligibility criterion for six-monthly clinical visits under the revised guidelines.

text.text: For these clients, we identified the first clinic visit following the scheduled VL test and calculated the interval between that visit and the next scheduled appointment using recorded appointment dates.
Clients with a scheduled appointment <168 days later were classified as having been assigned to <6-month visit intervals.
text.formatted: Clients with a scheduled appointment <168 days later were classified as having been assigned to <6-month visit intervals.

text.text: Clients with a scheduled appointment ≥168 days later were classified as having been assigned to ≥6-month visit intervals; those with no recorded clinic visit following their scheduled VL result were classified as having "no visit after VL result."
Clients who disengaged from care were classified using outcome status recorded in TIER.Net (death, loss to follow-up, or transfer to another facility).

At each stage of the cascade, clients with no recorded outcome and no subsequent clinic visits after the relevant milestone (first or second scheduled VL test) were classified as having disengaged from care as of their last observed visit.
We used descriptive statistics to summarise cohort characteristics, reporting frequencies and proportions.

Interrupted time-series (ITS) analyses assessed changes in two outcomes following implementation of the revised guidelines in April 2023: uptake of three-month viral load (VL) testing and assignment to extended clinic visit intervals (≥6 months).
The analysis populations differed according to the outcome being assessed.

The ITS analysis of threemonth VL testing included the eligible ART cohort, whereas the analysis of extended visit-interval assignment was restricted to clients with a suppressed VL result (<50 copies/mL) in the 3-month testing window, reflecting the revised guideline recommendation linking earlier viral suppression to eligibility for extended visit intervals.

text.text: Descriptive analyses of visit-interval assignment additionally included clients with a suppressed first scheduled VL result in either the 3-or 6-month testing window, allowing comparison of visit-interval assignment by timing of the first VL test.
The unit of analysis for both ITS outcomes was the district-quarter.

We modelled three distinct periods: pre-implementation (January 2022-March 2023), implementation (April-December 2023), and postimplementation (January 2024 onward), allowing each period to have its own level and trend.

Models were estimated separately by district using segmented linear regression of the quarterly proportion of clients with a VL result in the 3-month testing window and, for the second outcome, the quarterly proportion of virally suppressed clients assigned to extended (≥6-month) visit intervals.
Newey-West standard errors with a lag of 1 were used to account for autocorrelation.
The pre-implementation and implementation periods were consistent across both outcomes in King Cetshwayo and Ehlanzeni.
In these districts, the post-implementation period comprised six quarters (January 2024-June 2025).
In West Rand, where data were available for a shorter period, the postimplementation period comprised five quarters for 3-month VL testing and four quarters for visit-interval assignment.
We compared clients who received their first scheduled VL test during the 3-month window with those who received their first VL test during the 6-month window.

In this study of 16,338 adult South Africans who initiated ART since January 2022 , the introduction of early VL testing and earlier assignment to longer visit intervals was not associated with poorer subsequent virologic outcomes.
As intended, the 2023 ART guidelines were associated with rapid uptake of 3-month VL testing, earlier assignment to longer visit intervals, and fewer clinic visits during the first year on treatment.
Together, these findings suggest that earlier de-intensification of care can be implemented without sacrificing viral suppression among clients who achieve early viral suppression.
South Africa's experience demonstrates that early (three-month) VL testing is operationally feasible and can be implemented at scale within routine primary healthcare settings.
South Africa is not the only country to have moved towards earlier monitoring: Kenya's national guidelines have recommended 3month VL testing for ART initiators since 2022 (21).

text.text: Notably, however, Kenya's DSD eligibility criteria still require six months on treatment, separating earlier VL monitoring from early assignment to less intensive care.

Our finding that earlier VL testing combined with early assignment to longer prescribing and visit intervals was not associated with poorer subsequent outcomes supports the feasibility of allowing clients earlier access to differentiated care.
These findings should be interpreted with caution, however, as the observed changes followed guideline implementation but cannot be attributed to the guidelines alone.
In the absence of a comparison group, concurrent changes in service delivery or other factors may also have contributed to the observed trends.

Early assignment to longer visit intervals has previously been used pragmatically elsewhere in sub-Saharan Africa during periods of disruption, including the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak, armed conflict, and the COVID-19 pandemic, to maintain continuity of treatment while reducing facility contact (23).

text.text: Our findings provide evidence that early assignment to longer visit intervals can also be implemented in routine, non-emergency settings and that the historical requirement for clients to be on ART for 6 or 12 months before becoming eligible for DSD models (22) may not be necessary for clients who have achieved early viral suppression.

text.text: This study had several limitations.
First, approximately one quarter of clients had no documented VL test.

We cannot determine whether this reflects incomplete data capture in TIER.Net or incomplete VL testing, and our estimates of guideline fidelity may be biased if tests were performed according to guideline but were not captured in our data.
If missingness is due primarily to incomplete data capturethat is, tests were performed but not recorded-overall suppression could be higher than observed among clients with documented results.

If missingness is due largely to incomplete testing, results may instead overstate population-level suppression if failure to obtain a VL test is associated with treatment interruption or disengagement.
Furthermore, estimates of viral suppression were restricted to clients with documented VL results and may therefore not represent outcomes among all eligible clients.
If the likelihood of having a documented result is associated with retention in care, adherence, or clinical status, the observed suppression estimates may be subject to selection bias.
Second, because the TIER.Net DMOC enrolment field was incompletely captured, we relied on assignment to ≥6-month visit intervals as proxy measures of differentiated service delivery uptake.
These proxies may overestimate formal DMOC enrolment because clients can receive extended visit or dispensing intervals without enrolment in a DMOC.

Third, the study was conducted at 18 facilities in three districts, and, as such, our results may not be generalizable to other South African facilities and locations with different levels of implementation support, staffing, or infrastructure.

Fourth, although we adjusted the comparisons of visit interval and VL-testing timing for observed demographic and clinical characteristics, residual confounding by important unmeasured variables remains possible.

Clients assigned longer visit intervals may differ systematically from those assigned shorter intervals in characteristics not captured in routine data, including adherence history, clinical stability, or clinician assessment of readiness for differentiated care.
Fifth, analyses of viral suppression at the second scheduled VL test were necessarily restricted to clients with a documented second VL result.
Although availability of the second scheduled VL did not differ substantially by initial VL test timing, selection related to VL ascertainment cannot be excluded.

Finally, we were unable to distinguish reliably between ART-naïve initiators and clients re-initiating treatment and therefore could not assess whether the associations observed differed by prior ART exposure.
This may be particularly relevant to the preimplementation period, when earlier VL testing may have been more common among clients reinitiating treatment.

CONCLUSION South Africa's revised 2023 ART guidelines were associated with rapid uptake of earlier VL monitoring, earlier assignment to longer visit intervals, and fewer clinic visits during the first year of ART, although implementation remained incomplete.
Among clients with documented follow-up VL results, assignment to longer visit intervals was not associated with poorer subsequent viral suppression.
Continued efforts to improve implementation and VL documentation are warranted, alongside evaluation of longer-term retention and treatment outcomes.
